name: Silicon

claims.claim_text: A shared-wafer service such as MOSIS has long let a small organisation buy a custom chip outright for roughly ten to twenty thousand dollars of up-front non-recurring engineering, so a fully custom part has never been strictly out of reach for a determined small company; what is in question is whether the result earns that money back.
claims.quote_verbatim: you can go out and buy, you know, a chip for 10, $20,000 and have it manufactured, you know, some upfront NRE
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: China, Entrepreneurs and Blue Collar Reality

claims.claim_text: One of the few things that genuinely justifies putting a function on its own die is radio frequency performance: integrating an RF signal chain onto a single piece of silicon beats assembling the same function from discrete components on a board, because the parasitics of the board interconnect are removed.
claims.quote_verbatim: you can get better performance on a single, uh, silicon for say RF stuff than you can on, um, you know, just using discrete components on a board
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell
claims.episode_title: China, Entrepreneurs and Blue Collar Reality

claims.claim_text: A widely used alternative to spinning a custom part is to press an existing microcontroller into the role, since a general-purpose micro already carries the USB and UART blocks the job needs and is flexible enough to be reprogrammed; the counter-argument for a product team is that a pre-programmed, pre-tested off-the-shelf chip removes the work of programming and verifying the part yourself.
claims.quote_verbatim: instead of designing a custom chip to do that, custom silicon, just reuse an existing micro they've got because the micros are so flexible
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: Agilent, Analog, Cold Fusion - Funding Fusion Is Not Futile

claims.claim_text: The thermal steps are what make silicon processing uneconomic outside a factory. Running a furnace at around a thousand degrees Celsius for six hours consumes so much energy that a home-made solar cell will never generate back what it cost to make, even though the lithographic steps themselves are simple.
claims.quote_verbatim: run a furnace at 1,000 degrees C for six hours
claims.speaker: Jeri Ellsworth
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Jeri Ellsworth - Carnassial Chip Chemicals

claims.claim_text: A production fab escapes that energy penalty by never letting the furnaces cool: temperature is held continuously and wafers are fed through without interruption, which spreads the heating cost across an enormous number of parts and drives the energy cost per wafer down to fractions of a penny.
claims.quote_verbatim: If you have a factory where you keep the furnaces up to temperature and you're constantly feeding wafers in there, you can get that cost per BTU down
claims.speaker: Jeri Ellsworth
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Jeri Ellsworth - Carnassial Chip Chemicals

claims.claim_text: Making bipolar transistors demands much tighter furnace control than MOS does, because the emitter and collector diffusions have to meet the base in the middle: the process is governed jointly by temperature and time, and overrunning it consumes the base entirely, leaving a device with no base left.
claims.quote_verbatim: bipolars are a little bit more difficult at home because you need a furnace that's very accurate because you're doing a diffusion
claims.speaker: Jeri Ellsworth
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Jeri Ellsworth - Carnassial Chip Chemicals

claims.claim_text: MOSFETs are the easier device to build with crude equipment because the critical step is growing a gate oxide, and oxide thickness can be judged directly from the interference colour of the grown film rather than from instrumented measurement.
claims.quote_verbatim: it's much easier just to grow oxides for a MOSFET and just look at the color of the oxide to know that you've got the right thickness
claims.speaker: Jeri Ellsworth
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Jeri Ellsworth - Carnassial Chip Chemicals

claims.claim_text: High-integration mobile processors get their large memory by stacking: a DRAM die sits physically on top of the processor die and the two are packaged together as one component, which is why the part count on a phone board stays low while the memory does not.
claims.quote_verbatim: It's physically piggybacked on top of the silicon of the processor
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Jack Ganssle - Embedded Elchee Epexegesis

claims.claim_text: Function keeps migrating from the board down into the package and then into the die itself, by way of multi-chip modules, hybrid modules and flip chip assemblies, ending with everything on a single die; the direction of travel is steadily larger-scale integration.
claims.quote_verbatim: they're either pushing it all into multi-chip modules
claims.speaker: Henry Ott
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Henry Ott - Forced FCC Filtering

claims.claim_text: Memory is what makes a microcontroller expensive, not the processor core: the same part with 128k of memory instead of 32k costs substantially more because that memory occupies a large fraction of the die area, and die area is what is being sold.
claims.quote_verbatim: that memory space takes up a lot of die space
claims.speaker: Dave Jones

claims.claim_text: Embedded flash is a distinct process technology, so building it into a die raises the cost of the whole wafer. Leaving flash off the die and buying it from a dedicated flash maker is a real cost-optimisation lever, at the price of needing a second component.
claims.quote_verbatim: it does make the silicon cheaper if you don't have to build the Flash process into your silicon
claims.speaker: Dave Jones

claims.claim_text: Package size and die size are only loosely related. A part such as an ATmega328 in a DIP package is a very small piece of silicon inside a large moulded body, so the outline of a component says little about how much silicon has been bought.
claims.quote_verbatim: it was like tiny little bit of silicon with big old polymide
claims.speaker: Massimo Banzi
claims.episode_title: Arduino's Invisible Touch with Massimo Banzi

claims.claim_text: The long climb in serial link speeds has been driven chiefly by the transceiver silicon rather than by cables or connectors: as transistors shrink they switch faster, so shrinking is straightforwardly good for that application.
claims.quote_verbatim: The individual transistors inside can switch way faster than they ever could before because they're smaller
claims.speaker: Howard Johnson
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Dr. Howard Johnson - Winsome Waveform Wizardry

claims.claim_text: Devices reached hundreds of gigahertz through scaling alone. As geometries shrank, the intrinsic parasitic capacitances and other unwanted elements of the transistor shrank with them, to the point where building a transistor that generates signals in the hundreds of gigahertz became routine on a state-of-the-art process.
claims.quote_verbatim: Their intrinsic parasitic capacidences and unwanted components as part of devices have shrunk down and become so small that the devices become really, really fast
claims.speaker: Shahriar Shahramian
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Shahriar from The Signal Path - Quisquous Quivering Quadripole

claims.claim_text: Millimetre wave is conventionally taken to start around thirty gigahertz, the point where free-space wavelength falls below roughly ten millimetres, and inside silicon the wavelength is shorter still because of the dielectric: around ninety gigahertz it is about 1.6 millimetres with a dielectric constant near 4.2, which is what sets the physical size of on-die passive structures.
claims.quote_verbatim: I believe at 1.6 millimeter, it would be 90 gigahertz in silicon with an electric constant of 4.2
claims.speaker: Shahriar Shahramian
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Shahriar from The Signal Path - Quisquous Quivering Quadripole

claims.claim_text: A modern CMOS transistor is barely a silicon device any more. Germanium is added, the channel is strained, and a whole variety of other elements appear in the structure, so the physics of a 22 nanometre device is far more involved than that of an older 0.35 micron transistor.
claims.quote_verbatim: The CMOS transistor is almost barely is made of silicon anymore
claims.speaker: Shahriar Shahramian
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Shahriar from The Signal Path - Quisquous Quivering Quadripole

claims.claim_text: Yield on a die holding billions of devices is made acceptable by designing in redundancy, so that some fraction of the structures can fail without losing the part.
claims.quote_verbatim: there are some redundancies and so on, obviously, in there that allow some percentage of yield to be acceptable
claims.speaker: Shahriar Shahramian
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Shahriar from The Signal Path - Quisquous Quivering Quadripole

claims.claim_text: In silicon, electrons have higher mobility than holes, which is why N-channel MOSFETs are inherently better devices than P-channel ones; in organic semiconductors the ordering is often reversed, with holes the more mobile carrier.
claims.quote_verbatim: N-channel MOSFETs are inherently better than P-channel MOSFETs
claims.speaker: Sam Zeloof

claims.claim_text: Classical logic encodes information in the electrical state of a nanoscale transistor in silicon, with zeros and ones as low and high voltages. Building a doped device starts from a silicon crystal into which dopants such as phosphorus, arsenic or antimony are introduced.
claims.quote_verbatim: First you take a crystal of silicon and introduce dopants, which can be phosphorus or arsenic or antimony
claims.speaker: Andrea Morello

claims.claim_text: Silicon has a band gap in the low single digits of electron volts, whereas the wide band gap materials now in use, silicon carbide and gallium nitride, sit around three to four electron volts.
claims.quote_verbatim: Traditionally, people have used silicon, but silicon has a band gap in the low ones
claims.speaker: Paul Gulotta

claims.claim_text: The practical consequence of the wider band gap is switching speed: those devices can be turned on and off faster, which raises the switching frequency the whole downstream design can run at.
claims.quote_verbatim: they're able to achieve higher switching frequencies so they can be turned on faster
claims.speaker: Paul Gulotta

claims.claim_text: In a silicon switching converter it is the switching losses, not conduction losses, that set the ceiling on frequency, which is why wide band gap devices matter for power conversion.
claims.quote_verbatim: Because in silicon right now, the switching losses dominate
claims.episode_title: Moore's Law, GaN and SiC devices - Gallimaufry GaN Gabble

claims.claim_text: An implant or diffusion step never introduces only the intended species. While boron is being driven in, oxygen, nitrogen, helium, hydrogen and every other impurity present in the surrounding air go in with it, so the ambient atmosphere of the furnace is itself a process variable.
claims.quote_verbatim: as I'm implanting this boron, I'm implanting oxygen, nitrogen, helium, hydrogen, everything that's around you
claims.speaker: Sam Zeloof

claims.claim_text: Deliberately controlling the furnace ambient changes the electrical result: blowing chosen mixtures of nitrogen and oxygen through during the doping step dramatically alters the finished resistivity of the silicon.
claims.quote_verbatim: You can blow mixtures of, of nitrogen and oxygen into the furnace while you do this step. And that dramatically alters the resistivity of the silicon when you're done.
claims.speaker: Sam Zeloof

claims.claim_text: Nitrogen is used as the furnace purge precisely because it is the least harmful thing to incorporate: nitrogen embedded in silicon is not electrically active and does not shift device behaviour much, so displacing other impurities with nitrogen is a favourable trade.
claims.quote_verbatim: if you have nitrogen embedded into silicon, it's not going to be all that electrically reactive
claims.speaker: Sam Zeloof

claims.claim_text: Yield across a wafer depends on keeping process variation low everywhere on it. Where variation is not controlled the result is a bad die, and the area that die occupied is expensive silicon that has been thrown away.
claims.quote_verbatim: all your process variation has to be low across the wafer
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell
claims.episode_title: Hardware, Surveys and Giveaways - Radular Rental Ranting

claims.claim_text: Silicon's manufacturing advantage is defect density: it carries roughly a million times fewer defects than a typical perovskite film. At perovskite defect levels a silicon device would not work at all, because every carrier would be trapped.
claims.quote_verbatim: silicon has, um, about a million times fewer defects than, than a typical perovskite cell
claims.speaker: Sam Stranks

claims.claim_text: Overloading an output transistor produces a failure that spreads laterally through the die rather than staying local: the heat released at the device starts to break bonds, ions migrate under that heat, and the damage propagates across the silicon layer.
claims.quote_verbatim: the ions would start to migrate because of the heat starting to release some of their bonds
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell

claims.claim_text: Silicon is a weak absorber, so a silicon cell needs on the order of two hundred micrometres of material to capture the incident light. A perovskite film absorbs as strongly in a few hundred nanometres, roughly a four hundredfold reduction in material thickness.
claims.quote_verbatim: a few hundred nanometers of, of this film will absorb as much light as 200 microns of, of silicon
claims.speaker: Sam Stranks

claims.claim_text: Production capacity, not efficiency, is the binding constraint on silicon photovoltaics at global scale: running existing silicon panel manufacturing flat out would take forty to fifty years to reach world-scale deployment, which is the argument for thin-film alternatives that can be produced far faster.
claims.quote_verbatim: if we wanted to roll out enough silicon panels to power the world, um, at best it would take 40 to 50 years of just continually producing panels to get there
claims.speaker: Sam Stranks

claims.claim_text: Choosing a deliberately old process is a legitimate cost strategy. A field emission display programme was built in five micron NMOS specifically so that depreciated older equipment could be used, keeping costs low on a structure that did not need fine geometry.
claims.quote_verbatim: with the idea that we keep the costs low by using older equipment
claims.speaker: Jake Baker

claims.claim_text: The field emission display device worked by etching an emitter tip down into the silicon wafer, then laying glass and phosphor over the top with a metal grid positioned directly above the tip; the grid extracts electrons off the tip and they strike the phosphor to produce colour.
claims.quote_verbatim: you would put a layer of glass and phosphor on top with a metal grid right above the tip and it would extract the electrons off the tip
claims.speaker: Jake Baker

claims.claim_text: An old process node changes what is worth making. On a twenty-year-old process development kit there is no sensible reason to build a purely digital chip, because an off-the-shelf microcontroller will beat it; what such a node still offers is analogue and mixed signal capability.
claims.quote_verbatim: the PDK that I have access to is 20 years old
claims.speaker: Matt Venn

claims.claim_text: A fixed inference workload is a poor match for programmable logic: implementing it in an FPGA is costly in die area, in power, and in programming effort, whereas committing the same repeated computation to dedicated silicon removes all three costs.
claims.quote_verbatim: having an FPGA is obviously very expensive in terms of silicon and power
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell

claims.claim_text: The largest fabless companies break that symmetry by employing their own process technology engineers, who work directly with the foundry to develop process variants; the developing company then gets exclusive access to that process for something like a year before anyone else can use it.
claims.quote_verbatim: they have the people who develop technology on staff working one-on-one with the fabs coming up with custom process technology that maybe for the first year after it's been developed, they get exclusive access to it
claims.speaker: Philip Frieden
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Philip Freidin - Xenodochial Xilinx Ex-Employee

claims.claim_text: Some silicon is developed for only a handful of customers. Where an industry has half a dozen major players who each ship millions of units, a chip company will happily create a part for that tiny customer list, because unit volume rather than customer count is what pays for it.
claims.quote_verbatim: silicon would be developed for not more than like half a dozen customers
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: Google Glass & Adafruit - Obtaining Ostentatious Oculiforms

claims.claim_text: Entering silicon as a business is a hundred-million-dollar undertaking, and companies that fail at it typically end by selling off their design portfolio as assets rather than being bought as going concerns.
claims.quote_verbatim: a hundred million is what you need for you know getting into silicon
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell
claims.episode_title: Space Difficulties and Lost Heroes - Wanzing Workshop Whemmle

claims.claim_text: Chip lead times cannot be compressed below roughly eight weeks, because the material starts as sand and every process step is fixed in duration; that figure belongs in a schedule as a hard dependency with everything downstream moved out behind it.
claims.quote_verbatim: there is no possible way that we're going to get a chip in less than eight weeks
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell
claims.episode_title: Don't Turn It On, Don't Take It Apart

claims.claim_text: Restarting mothballed wafer capacity is far harder than it appears. Fabs that shut down had their capital equipment sold off rather than left idle, so what remains is an empty building and the restart is effectively from scratch.
claims.quote_verbatim: there's been fabs that have been slowly shutting down in the States over the years
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell

claims.claim_text: Academic computer architecture stalled as a build-it field because process advantage outran design advantage: a research chip taking four years to realise would be overtaken by a commercial part several times faster before it shipped.
claims.quote_verbatim: no one ever builds anything because Intel is just so good at building chips
claims.speaker: Bunnie Huang
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Bunnie Huang - Bunnie's Bibelot Bonification

claims.claim_text: When a process node stops yielding gains for analogue parts, innovation shifts into the package, and packaging then becomes the limiting factor until the next process jump arrives; the constraint moves rather than disappearing.
claims.quote_verbatim: when they run out of silicon stuff on a node, when they run out of, run out of juice, they start looking at packaging until they finally make a jump
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Bunnie Huang - Bunnie's Bibelot Bonification

claims.claim_text: A satellite connectivity business that requires its customers to design a new silicon modem into their own products faces an untenable go-to-market: each customer must commit to as much as eighteen months of prototyping and deployment on the promise that the network will exist when they finish.
claims.quote_verbatim: they were forcing their customers to have to embed a new silicon chip
claims.speaker: Alex Haro
claims.episode_title: Space Age Bluetooth with Alex Haro

claims.claim_text: A ten thousand dollar tape-out is inexpensive by the standards of a small or medium company, which makes low-cost shuttle runs a way to prove a concept before committing; once something works and has been characterised, the same company typically signs an NDA with a larger foundry for a finer process and licenses the commercial tools.
claims.quote_verbatim: even like $10,000 for a tape out is, is very cheap for, you know, a small to medium enterprise
claims.speaker: Matt Venn
claims.episode_title: Open Source Tapeout with Matthew Venn

claims.claim_text: A ten thousand dollar shuttle run historically returned somewhere between one hundred and fifty and two hundred packaged chips, which is a prototyping quantity rather than a production one.
claims.quote_verbatim: Somewhere between 150 and 200 chips back
claims.speaker: Tim Ansell

claims.claim_text: A thousand chips changes the category of the service: enough parts remain after two prototype board revisions of a hundred units each to ship five hundred units of product, so the run functions as low volume production rather than as prototyping.
claims.quote_verbatim: a thousand chips is enough that you can actually think of it as low volume production, not as a prototyping service
claims.speaker: Tim Ansell

claims.claim_text: The cost arithmetic that makes a low-volume custom part viable runs through the usual three-times bill-of-materials rule: at seven dollars a chip inside a thirty to forty dollar bill of materials, the product retails near a hundred dollars and the custom silicon is affordable within it.
claims.quote_verbatim: seven bucks a chip means these products owe a hundred dollar products based on the, you know, three times bomb cost
claims.speaker: Tim Ansell

claims.claim_text: Turnaround on a shared shuttle run is around nine months from design submission to receiving parts, and the parts come back packaged rather than as bare die.
claims.quote_verbatim: Nine months to get my ASIC back
claims.speaker: Dave Jones

claims.claim_text: A sensible split for a first custom part is to keep it digital. High-precision analogue such as a chopper-stabilised amplifier is the wrong thing to attempt on a low-cost shuttle process, whereas a small custom processor block is a reasonable target.
claims.quote_verbatim: I wouldn't do analog there
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: The Joulescope Upgrade with Matt Liberty

claims.claim_text: A silicon interposer avoids per-customer custom silicon by keeping the underlying transistors identical for everyone and configuring only the connectivity: the customer's schematic is burned into the interposer as a switch configuration that wires the chiplets together the required way.
claims.quote_verbatim: the underlying transistors in the silicon interposer are common
claims.speaker: Ming Zhang

claims.claim_text: Silicon offers no equivalent of a bodge wire. A board can be corrected after fabrication with a cut trace and a jumper, but an error committed to a die cannot be patched, which is a large part of why an off-the-shelf part is easier for a small team working to an aggressive schedule.
claims.quote_verbatim: there's no bodge wires in silicon
claims.speaker: Dave Jones

claims.claim_text: A chip that does not start up correctly may be a design fault or a part fault, and the questions that settle it are often not answerable from the datasheet: whether particular pins must be tied a certain way, or whether they carry internal pull-ups.
claims.quote_verbatim: maybe there are some pins that I don't know if they need to be tied a certain direction or if they've got internal pull-ups or something like that
claims.speaker: Jeff Keyzer

claims.claim_text: Manufacturing in China gives a design team a support channel that has no equivalent elsewhere: almost any component problem can be resolved within a day or two by bringing a local manufacturer's representative in to provide support in person.
claims.quote_verbatim: there seems to be no issue that within one or two days cannot be solved by bringing in like a local manufacturer's representative
claims.speaker: Jeff Keyzer

claims.claim_text: On a compressed schedule the pinout of a new chip may still be unfixed while the die is already in fabrication, because bond-out is decided later than the die itself; a board team designing to a provisional pinout is accepting real risk and does it only when the timeline leaves no choice.
claims.quote_verbatim: the silicon might go, you mightn't even have the pin out finalized
claims.speaker: Kieran O'Leary

claims.claim_text: Boards come back faster than chips do, so schematic capture and layout for the target board should begin as the silicon goes to fabrication or even before, with normal schematic and layout reviews still applied.
claims.quote_verbatim: your PCB will come back quicker than the silicon
claims.speaker: Kieran O'Leary

claims.claim_text: First silicon typically arrives untested, because a test engineer needs physical samples to validate the test program before it can be deployed to the assembly site; the parts and the means of testing them are not ready at the same moment.
claims.quote_verbatim: these chips are coming back and they won't have been tested
claims.speaker: Kieran O'Leary

claims.claim_text: Bringing up untested parts often needs a custom socket, and those sockets run into thousands of dollars each, particularly for fine-pitch ball grid array packages where alignment must be exact.
claims.quote_verbatim: those sockets can run to thousands of dollars
claims.speaker: Kieran O'Leary

claims.claim_text: Partitioning a system across two dies can be the right answer when the two halves want different things: the large processor die stays generic while the medium-speed mixed-signal interfaces such as USB and GPIO move into a second, separately controlled chip that the system owner can specify exactly.
claims.quote_verbatim: it makes a lot of sense for us to put our specific Raspberry Pi things in a separate bit of silicon, which we can control
claims.speaker: James Adams
claims.episode_title: The RP1 and beyond with the Raspberry Pi Hardware team

claims.claim_text: Owning the silicon lets the pinout be co-designed with the board: every chip on the board can have its pins placed so the wires leave in exactly the right direction. On a multi-lane PCI Express link between two chips, differential pairs that had to cross over would force a more expensive board technology.
claims.quote_verbatim: every chip has been co-designed or designed to have the pins and the wires coming out in exactly the right place
claims.speaker: James Adams
claims.episode_title: The RP1 and beyond with the Raspberry Pi Hardware team

claims.claim_text: Owning the silicon in an instrument is a durable competitive position, since a rival cannot simply produce a cheaper version of the same architecture. The counterweight is that a competitor building from off-the-shelf parts can still reach a comparable specification at a low price.
claims.quote_verbatim: that is a competitive advantage, is having custom silicon
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell

claims.claim_text: Designing for volume means pulling as much as possible onto a small number of chips: one sensor unit carrying all the inertial measurement, one processor, drivers pushed out to the motors, and almost nothing else on the board.
claims.quote_verbatim: That's how they're going to get the $49 price point
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: Boeing, PCBs & Startups - Awful Airplane Aeration

claims.claim_text: When a die is thinned from the back for inspection, the material being removed is essentially pure silicon; the only doping at that depth is the wafer's own background doping and possibly some very deep implants, since the active structures sit far shallower.
claims.quote_verbatim: there might be some doping from like really deep implanted dopants
claims.speaker: Dmitry Nedospasov

claims.claim_text: Under X-ray inspection silicon is largely transparent while metal is easy to see, so adjusting the contrast changes which structures appear: bond wires are extremely fine and the gold shows differently to other materials, which lets the internal redistribution board inside a module be traced separately from the die above it.
claims.quote_verbatim: The silicon kind of seemed pretty transparent to these rays
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell

claims.claim_text: Building a three-dimensional model of the process layers, with each layer labelled and independently hideable, teaches device structure far better than the conventional top-down and cross-section drawings, because it supplies the view between the two that textbook figures never give.
claims.quote_verbatim: We put together Google SketchUp of the different layers in Silicon where we were able to label everything, hide everything
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell
claims.episode_title: Wrong Hardware, Wrong Software - Fugacious Fan Funding

claims.claim_text: Silicon cost can dominate a product outright. One development board retailed at twenty-five thousand dollars because the chip on it cost so much, with sixteen thousand dollars of that being the cost to populate the board, making a build of a hundred units a serious financial commitment.
claims.quote_verbatim: when we first retailed it, it was $25,000. Because a silicon was cost, and it's like $16,000 just to populate the board.
claims.speaker: Clint Cole
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Clint Cole of Digilent

claims.claim_text: A spacecraft instrument power budget of around fifty watts leaves only one to two watts for the digital back end, which rules out an FPGA and forces dedicated silicon for a signal-processing chain running four thousand to eight thousand point transforms behind a six gigasample-per-second converter.
claims.quote_verbatim: your instrument power budget might only be 50 watts, which means, you know, forget the FPGAs
claims.speaker: Adrian Tang

attribution_notes: Passage speakers were re-derived by locating each quote in the episode transcript and reading the nearest preceding **Speaker:** label; where that label disagreed with the bundle header, the transcript label was used unless the content plainly identified someone else.

Episodes 279 and 44-index passages: the transcript labels the teardown-markings, China-support and chip-bring-up material as Chris Gammell, but the content is the guest describing his own product, his own team and his own experiences in China, so it is attributed to Jeff Keyzer (the episode 279 guest).

Episode 390 carries a corrupted diarization label ('Arduinos') on the doping and mobility answers; the content is the guest describing his own home fabrication process, so it is attributed to Sam Zeloof.

Episodes 433, 452, 297, 302, 303, 616 and 483 label technical answers as Chris Gammell where the content is unmistakably the guest describing their own research, company or process; these are attributed to Sam Stranks, Kieran O'Leary, Jake Baker, Clint Cole, Dmitry Nedospasov, Matt Venn and Adrian Tang respectively.

Episode 534 attributes the wide band gap material to Paul Gulotta of Mouser Electronics, who is introduced by name as the speaker in that segment, rather than to the host label carried in the transcript.

Episode 52 labels the guest as 'Jerry Ellsworth'; the name is given here as Jeri Ellsworth. Episode 228 labels 'Shariar' and is given as Shahriar Shahramian; episode 84 labels 'Bunny' and is given as Bunnie Huang; episode 570 labels 'Jeff Kaiser' and is given as Jeff Keyzer.
Episode 61's switching-loss remark is labelled 'Sydney', an unresolved diarization label, and the content does not identify the speaker, so no speaker is recorded.
Episode 607's chopper-amplifier exchange is flagged unreliable and the labels appear shifted; only the reply that the transcript places unambiguously after a Dave Jones label is used.
Passage index 0 (episode 41, the 22 nanometre gate discussion) was not cited: the text could not be located anywhere in that episode's transcript, so the passage appears to be misaligned.
